summary: A modular monolith build: Server-rendered HTML + HTMX on the frontend, C# + ASP.NET Core for the backend, Microsoft SQL Server for data, hosted on Azure App Service for about $23-180 a month. It keeps the existing Microsoft SQL Server data (moved to Azure SQL Database) and Microsoft Entra ID sign-in, stays on Azure and keeps data in India under ISO 27001, builds on the team's C#/.NET, and ships as one deployable that a team of 2 can build in 6 weeks.

frontend.justification: Server-rendered HTML + HTMX is the frontend for an Internal tool / admin panel project with about 300 daily users (~1.6 requests/s at peak), built by a team of 2 in 6 weeks. Its strongest weighted criterion for your answers is low ops burden: 5.0/5 at weight 4.0, the largest share of its score. It leads the runner-up, React SPA (Vite), by 1.4 points (out of 100 on the whole-stack score, the average of the four layer scores).

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 1.4 points. Server-rendered HTML + HTMX is stronger on team skill match (4.5 vs 3.5), learning curve (5.0 vs 4.0); React SPA (Vite) is stronger on ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 3.0), rich client interactivity (5.0 vs 2.0). 1.3 of the 1.4 points come from a stack compatibility rule: The backend renders HTML fragments directly: one codebase, no API layer or SPA build.

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.2 points. Server-rendered HTML + HTMX is stronger on learning curve (5.0 vs 3.0), low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0); Next.js (React) is stronger on development speed (5.0 vs 4.0), ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 3.0); Next.js (React) takes a penalty: No search visibility needed: server rendering adds a Node.js server for pages that React SPA (Vite) serves as static files. 1.3 of the 3.2 points come from a stack compatibility rule: The backend renders HTML fragments directly: one codebase, no API layer or SPA build.

tradeoffs: Structure for large teams is only 2.0/5 (weight 1.0).
Rich client interactions (drag-drop editors, offline) get awkward
Requires a server-rendering backend; does not pair with BaaS

backend.justification: C# + ASP.NET Core serves the API at about 1.6 requests/s at peak (Small (50-500 users online at once)) for a team of 2. The team lists C#/.NET, so it needs no new server language (team skill match 4.5/5). It runs as a long-running C#/.NET service, so background jobs and database connection pools live in one deployable process. It leads the runner-up, PHP + Laravel, by 3.7 points. It works with the existing Microsoft SQL Server for data and Microsoft Entra ID for sign-in.

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.7 points. C# + ASP.NET Core is stronger on team skill match (4.5 vs 3.5), learning curve (5.0 vs 4.0); PHP + Laravel is stronger on development speed (5.0 vs 4.0). 2.0 of the 3.7 points come from a stack compatibility rule: First-party tooling (Visual Studio publish, Entra ID, Application Insights).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 5.1 points. C# + ASP.NET Core is stronger on structure for large teams (5.0 vs 1.0), performance / latency (5.0 vs 3.0); Node.js + Express is stronger on hiring pool (5.0 vs 4.0). 2.0 of the 5.1 points come from a stack compatibility rule: First-party tooling (Visual Studio publish, Entra ID, Application Insights).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 7.8 points. C# + ASP.NET Core is stronger on team skill match (4.5 vs 1.5), learning curve (5.0 vs 4.0); Python + Django is stronger on development speed (5.0 vs 4.0); Python + Django takes a penalty: Nobody on the team listed Python or a closely related skill: a new server language to learn. 2.0 of the 7.8 points come from a stack compatibility rule: First-party tooling (Visual Studio publish, Entra ID, Application Insights).
Ruled out: Not on Azure, the cloud you require; No ISO/IEC 27001 certification published

tradeoffs: Ecosystem is centred on Microsoft tooling

database.choice: Microsoft SQL Server: Azure SQL Database (General Purpose, serverless or provisioned)
database.justification: Your data is mainly relational and reaches about 3.4 GB within 12 months; Microsoft SQL Server fits relational data 5/5. Strong consistency is assumed, since no input says stale reads are acceptable, and Microsoft SQL Server gives it: a read after a write always sees that write. Its share of the estimated bill is $8-$24 a month, against a total budget of $300 a month. It leads the runner-up, PostgreSQL, by 2.0 points.

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 2.0 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on portability (low lock-in) (5.0 vs 3.0), hiring pool (5.0 vs 4.0).
Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 2.1 points. MySQL is stronger on portability (low lock-in) (5.0 vs 3.0), hiring pool (5.0 vs 4.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 12.0 points. Microsoft SQL Server is stronger on data-model fit (5.0 vs 2.0), consistency fit (5.0 vs 3.5); MongoDB is stronger on scalability (5.0 vs 4.0), portability (low lock-in) (4.0 vs 3.0); MongoDB takes a penalty: Only 2/5 fit for your primary 'relational' data.
Ruled out: Not on Azure, the cloud you require

tradeoffs: Commercial licence: managed instances cost more than PostgreSQL or MySQL of the same size
T-SQL and its features are specific to SQL Server, so moving off it is a migration

hosting.choice: Azure App Service, region Central India (Pune)
hosting.justification: Azure App Service hosts the stack for users in India at a 99.9% availability target. It runs the C# + ASP.NET Core API as long-running processes, sized for ~1.6 requests/s at peak. It has a region in India, so data can stay in the country. Its share of the estimated bill is $15-$156 a month, against a total budget of $300 a month.

alternatives.why_not: Ruled out for your answers: Not on Azure, the cloud you require.
Ruled out for your answers: Not on Azure, the cloud you require.

tradeoffs: Portal/config complexity; pricing tiers are confusing

supporting.justification: Send emails, process uploads and call slow APIs outside the request path. Sized for the 1,500 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: Fixed schedules only: no retries, no priorities and nothing started by a user's action

alternatives.choice: Doing the work inside the web request
alternatives.why_not: Slow emails, uploads and API calls would hold the request open and fail with it

tradeoffs: A job can run twice after a retry, so handlers must be idempotent

supporting.choice: Blob Storage, a private container in your required region with short-lived SAS URLs, without Front Door (no public Microsoft page lists Front Door's audit scope)
supporting.justification: Uploaded files and video belong in object storage, not the database. The scenario stores 20 GB within 12 months (scale.data_volume_gb_12_months).

alternatives.choice: Files on the app server's disk
alternatives.why_not: Lost when an instance is replaced, and not shared between instances
They bloat backups and the database disk, which costs several times more per GB than object storage

tradeoffs: Files and their database rows can drift apart: delete or replace both together

supporting.choice: Microsoft Entra ID (existing), signed in through OpenID Connect
supporting.justification: infrastructure.existing_systems lists Microsoft Entra ID: users sign in with the accounts it already manages, so there is no new user store, MFA and password rules come from it, and removing someone there removes their access here. Sized for the 1,500 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.choice: Your backend framework's built-in authentication, with the users in your database in India
alternatives.why_not: A second identity system to run beside Microsoft Entra ID, which already holds the users

tradeoffs: Sign-in depends on Microsoft Entra ID being reachable

supporting.choice: OpenTelemetry instrumentation -> Azure Monitor Application Insights
supporting.justification: Traces, metrics and error tracking from day one; required to defend an availability target. A 99.9% availability target (requirements.availability) allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month, so failures must show within minutes.

alternatives.why_not: They show the app is down, not why
Without traces and metrics there is no way to see which call is slow or failing

tradeoffs: Telemetry volume is billed: sample traces and set log retention

supporting.justification: Every push runs the tests and deploys the same way; hosted runners mean no build server to operate. All 2 engineers (team.size) release through the same pipeline.

alternatives.why_not: Equivalent pipelines; one more tool to learn for no gain here

alternatives.choice: Deploying by hand from a developer's machine
alternatives.why_not: No test gate, and each release depends on one person's setup

tradeoffs: Pipeline minutes are metered on hosted runners

assumptions: Planning estimate from published price bands at your scale tier, each read where the project sits inside its tier, with the usage terms listed per line; excludes salaries, third-party SaaS (auth, email, payments fees) and egress spikes.
Scale tier: Small (50-500 users online at once)

Hosting: Azure App Service: $15-156 (Small (50-500 users online at once) price band, from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for 300 users online at once (78% of the way up the tier, log scale); one instance carries Azure App Service's 99.95% SLA, which meets the 99.9% target, so no second instance is priced)

Database: Microsoft SQL Server: $8-24 (Hobby (one tier below the traffic: read-heavy, caches absorb most reads) database tier (~3 GB in 12 months), from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for ~3 GB of data (53% of the way up the tier, log scale); x1.5 for 99.9% availability (standby/replicas))
Object storage: $0-0 (~17 GB of uploaded files (the stated total less the database's ~3 GB) at $0.0196-0.0208/GB-month (https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/storage/blobs/))

warnings.message: 'On-prem SQL Server 2019': SQL Server 2019 is in extended support: security updates only, until 8 Jan 2030 (https://learn.microsoft.com/lifecycle/products/sql-server-2019). Keeping it is fine; schedule the upgrade before that date.

assumptions: project.description sets no field in a scenario file: every choice comes from the structured fields, so wording cannot move the stack (in the app, the description reader only suggests fields for you to confirm); a fixed keyword list adds the 'Read from project.description' notes, which change no pick
Sized for scale.users_12_months: 1,500 users, about 300 active on a day (20% daily-to-monthly ratio); scale.users_at_launch (1,200) is the starting point
iso27001: only hosts and managed services (backend-as-a-service, managed-only databases) that publish ISO/IEC 27001 certification are kept
Priorities rated 4 or 5 raise their criteria's weights, strongest first: time_to_market (5), maintainability (5), security (4)
Priorities rated 1 or 2 (scalability, performance) keep their criteria at the baseline weight
Existing identity provider Microsoft Entra ID: sign-in reuses it through OpenID Connect or SAML instead of a new user store

Existing database 'On-prem SQL Server 2019': Microsoft SQL Server is weighed with a bonus for keeping it; if it stays the pick, move its data to the recommended offering with the vendor's migration tool, or reach it over a private link (site-to-site VPN) while it stays where it is
Existing system 'Microsoft 365': integrated through Microsoft Graph API (mail, calendar and Teams notifications, files); it stays the system of record for its own data

Questionnaire answers the scenario schema has no field for took their defaults: data_shapes 'relational', consistency 'strong', architecture 'auto', lock_in_tolerance 'medium' (an extensions block can set them)

Stored data: The stated 20 GB counts uploaded files too. The database is sized for ~3.40 GB of rows (0.5 MB per daily user a month for this app type, at ~533 daily users, launch plus 12 months), and the other ~17 GB of files is priced as object storage on the stack's cloud.
